newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong inflation fall masks trend - economists.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong inflation fall masks trend - economists.

text.p: Hong Kong's consumer price index fell to 5.7 percent year-on-year in March, down from 6.5 percent in February, but economists warned on Tuesday that the underlying trend was still upwards.

The Census and Statistics Department said that the slower year-on-year increase in March was attributable to year-on-year declines in the prices of some fresh foods and slower increases in the cost of meals bought away from home.
NatWest Markets assistant economist Arthur Woo said the figure surprised him, and predicted a pickup in prices.
"The trend in consumer prices is definitely upwards," said Woo, who forecast a 6.8 percent rise for 1997 overall.
Consumer prices rose by just 6.0 percent in 1996.
Economists said the fall in the March figures also reflected a good mainland harvest, cutting down the cost of the food imported daily from China.
"You're talking about the classical economic environment where supply exceeds demand," TDC assistant chief economist Mike Martin told Reuters.
Martin said a strong U.S. dollar had helped keep transport costs down, and lower inflation in China had also helped keep Hong Kong inflation lower.
But he said said longer-term questions about Hong Kong's inflation rate remained. "Is Hong Kong pricing itself out of competitiveness?" he said.
Excluding the food component, inflation was seven percent in the March quarter, up from 6.5 percent in the December quarter, HongkongBank senior economist Clarence Wong said
"Underlying inflation, actually, is still on an upward trend," said Wong, tipping 6.8 percent inflation for the territory in calendar 1997.
Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce chief economist Ian Perkin said the March figures were "a good start to the year".
Perkin expects six percent inflation in 1997, adding that five percent was achievable if interest rates rose.
Economists expressed concern that the strong property market would keep upward pressure on inflation -- housing costs rose by 9.2 percent year-on-year in March.
Eddie Wong, ABN AMRO-Hoare Govett regional economist, said residential leases renewals this year could boost inflation, forecasting 6.6 percent inflation for Hong Kong in 1997.
